passages.happening:
On the plains of Moab God gives Moses another instruction for life in the land. “Command the Israelites to give, from the inheritance they will possess, cities for the Levites to live in and pasturelands around the cities” (verse 2).

The pasture is to reach out from each town on every side (verses 4-5). There are to be forty-eight towns in all, and six of them are to be cities of refuge (verses 6-7). They are to be given ‘in proportion to the inheritance of each tribe: more from a larger tribe and less from a smaller one’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 34 drew the borders of the land. One tribe was left out of the sharing. The Levites were counted apart in the census ‘because no inheritance was given to them’ (26:62). God had said that he himself was their share. This chapter says where they will live.

They are given towns, with grazing land around them for their animals. They are not given a territory. And the towns are drawn from every tribe. The result is that the Levites are scattered through the whole land on purpose. The tribe charged with teaching God's law and serving at his sanctuary will have neighbors in every part of Israel.

Each tribe gives according to what it has received, more from the large and less from the small. Every tribe makes room, on its own land, for people whose work is the worship of God.

The two measurements for the pasture, a thousand cubits in verse 4 and two thousand in verse 5, have puzzled readers, and several ways of fitting them together have been proposed. The text does not explain.

The book of Joshua lists the forty-eight towns by name (Joshua 21). Some have been identified with known sites. Scholars debate whether that list reflects the time of Joshua or a later period.
passages.later:
Long before, Jacob had said of his sons Simeon and Levi, after an act of violence, “I will disperse them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Genesis 49:7). For Levi the scattering became a calling. Moses later said of Levi, “He will teach Your ordinances to Jacob and Your law to Israel” (Deuteronomy 33:10).

Joshua records that it was done: “So by the command of the LORD, the Israelites gave the Levites these cities and their pasturelands out of their own inheritance” (Joshua 21:3).
passages.asks: Every tribe gave up some of its own land so that people who served God could live among them. Ask what room you make, in your budget and your neighborhood, for those whose work is to teach and to serve. And ask whether the place where you have been scattered might be a calling.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses, “When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan, designate cities to serve as your cities of refuge, so that a person who kills someone unintentionally may flee there” (verses 10-11).

“You are to have these cities as a refuge from the avenger, so that the manslayer will not die until he stands trial before the assembly” (verse 12).

There are to be six, three on each side of the Jordan (verse 14). “These six cities will serve as a refuge for the Israelites and for the foreigner or stranger among them” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This law deals with one of the gravest problems of any settled people. One person has killed another. What happens next?

In Israel, as across the ancient world, there was no police force. When someone was killed, the duty of seeing justice done fell on the victim's family. The nearest male relative was called the avenger of blood. The Hebrew word is go'el. It is the same word used for the relative who bought back family land, or who freed a family member from slavery. His task was to restore what the family had lost. After a killing, that meant going after the killer.

The danger is plain. A grieving relative does not stop to ask whether the death was an accident. An axe-head flies off its handle and a man dies, and before nightfall his brother has killed the one who was holding the axe. Then that man's family has a death to avenge. That is how a feud begins.

The cities of refuge break the chain. A person who has killed can run to one of them and be safe inside its walls until the case is heard. Verse 12 states the principle: no one is to die until he has stood trial. The law does not do away with the family's part in justice. It places a court between the killing and the punishment.

Notice who is covered. The refuge is for ‘the Israelites and for the foreigner or stranger among them’. An outsider with no clan to protect him had the same right to a hearing as anyone else.

There were six, three on each side of the river, spread out so that no one would be far from one. The book of Joshua names them: Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron in the west, and Bezer, Ramoth and Golan in the east (Joshua 20:7-8). All six were towns of the Levites.

The Hebrew word for ‘refuge’ here, miqlat, is used in the Old Testament only of these cities. It seems to come from a root that means to take in.
passages.later:
The law had promised such a place from the beginning. In Exodus God says of the person who kills without lying in wait, “then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee” (Exodus 21:13).

The Psalms speak of God himself as a refuge, with other Hebrew words: “God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble” (Psalm 46:1).

Hebrews uses the picture of people who have ‘fled to take hold of the hope set before us’ (Hebrews 6:18). Many Christian readers have seen in the cities of refuge a picture of Christ as the place of safety. That is a likeness later readers have drawn. Numbers does not predict it.
passages.asks: The law put a hearing between a death and its punishment, and gave the stranger the same right to it as the citizen. Ask how quickly you pass sentence when you hear that someone has done wrong. And ask who near you has no one to stand up for them, and where they could run.

passages.t: Murder, and a death no one meant
passages.happening:
The law sets out how to tell the two apart. If someone strikes another with an iron object, a stone big enough to kill, or a wooden weapon, and the person dies, ‘he is a murderer’ (verses 16-18). So is anyone who kills out of hatred, by a push, a thrown object or a blow of the hand (verses 20-21). In those cases the murderer is to be put to death.

“But if anyone pushes a person suddenly, without hostility, or throws an object at him unintentionally, or without looking drops a heavy stone that kills him, but he was not an enemy and did not intend to harm him, then the congregation must judge between the slayer and the avenger of blood” (verses 22-24).

“The assembly is to protect the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood” (verse 25). He is sent back to the city of refuge and must live there ‘until the death of the high priest’. If he leaves it before then, the avenger may kill him (verses 26-28).
passages.hearers:
The Hebrew verb for killing in this chapter is the one in the commandment “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). Here it is used both for murder and for a death no one intended. The whole work of the law is to tell them apart.

It does so by evidence. What was in the person's hand? A tool that could be expected to kill points to intent. Was there hatred beforehand? Did he lie in wait? Or did it happen ‘suddenly’, ‘without hostility’, ‘without looking’? The court is to weigh the weapon, the history between the two, and the purpose. These are the questions a court still asks.

The decision belongs to the assembly, the community acting as a court. It does not belong to the avenger, and it does not belong to the killer.

A person found to have killed by accident is protected. But he does not simply go home. He must live in the city of refuge until the high priest dies. That is a real loss: years away from his land and his people. The law does not treat a death as nothing because no one meant it. A life has been lost, and it weighs something even where there is no guilt of murder.

Why the death of the high priest? The text does not say. It seems to have marked a turning point, after which the matter was closed and the man could go home. Many interpreters think the death of the anointed priest was understood to settle, in some way, the matter of the blood that had been shed.

A reader who has caused a death by accident, on the road or at work or in the home, may find these verses heavy. They are also merciful. The law knows the difference between what a person did and what a person meant. It does not call such a person a murderer, and it gives them a place to live and a day when it will be over.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy gives an example of the kind of case in view: a man goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut timber, and as he swings his axe ‘the blade flies off the handle and strikes and kills his neighbor’ (Deuteronomy 19:5).

Hebrews speaks of a high priest whose death opens a way: “where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 6:20). Some Christian readers have seen the release at the high priest's death as a picture of the freedom won by the death of Christ. That too is a likeness drawn later, and it should not be pressed further than that.
passages.hard:
The murderer ‘must surely be put to death’. Does this chapter require the death penalty today?

This was the law of ancient Israel, given for a nation living in its land under the covenant of Sinai. It was hedged with protections: a trial before the community, careful tests of intent, and more than one witness (verse 30).

On whether governments should take life for murder now, Christians differ. Many hold that they should. They point to God's word to Noah, long before the law of Moses, “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind” (Genesis 9:6), and to Paul's saying that the ruler ‘does not carry the sword in vain’ (Romans 13:4). Many others hold that these texts state how grave murder is, because life is sacred, without requiring every state in every age to take a life, and they note that God himself protected Cain (Genesis 4:15). These notes do not settle it.

Every side agrees on two things. The law's reason is the worth of the person who was killed. And the role of the avenger of blood belonged to a world without police or public courts. Nothing here permits any family or any person today to take revenge for a death.
passages.asks: The law weighed what a person intended, and still did not treat an accidental death as nothing. Ask whether you carry guilt for a harm you never meant, and whether you have let anyone help you carry it. And ask whether you hold others to account for what they intended, or only for what resulted.

passages.happening:
Three rules close the law. “But no one is to be put to death based on the testimony of a lone witness” (verse 30). “You are not to accept a ransom for the life of a murderer who deserves to die” (verse 31). And no payment may buy the release of a man from the city of refuge before the high priest's death (verse 32).

Then comes the reason. “Do not pollute the land where you live, for bloodshed pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land on which the blood is shed, except by the blood of the one who shed it. Do not defile the land where you live and where I dwell. For I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites” (verses 33-34).
passages.hearers:
These last verses show what the whole chapter has been protecting.

The rule about witnesses protects the accused. No one may be put to death on one person's word. A single accuser may be mistaken, or may be lying. In a chapter about taking life seriously, the life of the person on trial is taken seriously too.

The rule about ransom protects the worth of the victim. Some other law collections of the ancient world, the Hittite laws among them, allowed a killing to be settled by payment. Israel's law refuses. If money could settle a murder, a rich man could kill and pay, and a poor man's life would have a price that a rich man could afford. The law says that no sum is equal to a human life. The reason goes back to the beginning of the Bible: every person is made in the image of God (Genesis 9:6).

The same rule applies to the man in the city of refuge. He cannot buy his way home early. Rich and poor wait alike.

Then the chapter gives its deepest reason, and it is about the land. Innocent blood pollutes the ground it falls on. The Hebrew word means to profane. A land where killing goes unanswered is a spoiled land.

And it matters because of who lives there. The final sentence takes the reader back to the start of the book. In chapter 5 the camp had to be kept clean because God lived in it. Now it is the whole land. ‘I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites.’ Every human life is to be guarded because God has made his home among his people.
passages.later:
The first murder in the Bible is told in the same terms. God says to Cain, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10).

Jesus took the commandment behind this chapter further back, to its root in the heart: ‘anyone who is angry with his brother will be subject to judgment’ (Matthew 5:22).

Hebrews sets the blood of Jesus beside the blood that cries out from the ground: believers have come ‘to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel’ (Hebrews 12:24).
passages.asks: The law refused to let any life be paid for with money, and required more than one witness before a person could be condemned. Ask whose lives are treated as cheaper than others in the place where you live. And ask what it would change in your street or your city to believe that God lives there, and that every person in it bears his image.
